verses.verse:
आवृत्तिस्तु स्वरैके स्वयाद् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रये भवेल्लंघः संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०५।
verses.text: Āvṛtti (repetition) is in one note; vaiparītya (reversal) in two notes; in three notes there is laṅgha (leaping); and sañcāra (movement) in four.

commentary.text: Āvṛtti (repetition) means repeating a note again and again. But if a group of two or three notes is repeated, understand it as dvayāvṛtti (two-note repetition) and trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition) respectively.

commentary.table_html:
Kinds of āvṛtti (repetition)
Ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition)Dvayāvṛtti (two-note repetition)Trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition)
Sa Sa SaSaRe SaReSaReGa SaReGa

commentary.text: This is a simple quality, which is ordinarily possible in anything from one note to many notes. But repetition of more than three is impractical. A somewhat more precious quality lies in two notes: vaiparītya (reversal), that is, being turned over, and being smaller and larger. This quality is impossible in one note, just as, if someone has only one son, it is impossible to decide whether he is the younger or the elder. More precious still is the quality that lives in three notes, or in more than three notes: laṅghita (leaping), that is, leaving out some note in between and going on to a note further ahead. For example, 'Sa Ga'.

Better still is the quality that lives in four notes: (sañcāra) wandering. All the qualities above are possible in many alaṅkāras (patterned exercises); even so, in a given alaṅkāra one quality is found to predominate. For example -

commentary.text: In the same way, on the basis of just three notes, alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) can be made from Dādarā up to Tīntāl, that is, from six mātrās (beats) to 16 mātrās. Making orders of notes according to the short and long syllables in words is called śabdānukaraṇa (imitation of words). If someone spoke a word (paṅkaja), we should understand it as paṃ - ka ja, because uttering paṃ takes more time than 'ka' and 'ja'. Following it, [the notes] will be Sa - Re Ga. Now more examples are presented.

commentary.text: Thoughtful sādhakas (practitioners) make many alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) by mixing, on the basis of these qualities. Here some practical alaṅkāras are presented as examples. The various svara-śaktis (powers of the notes) contained in them, readers will themselves recognize in the form of seeds, and will use them. These alaṅkāras are built in two notes up to four notes. Their length ranges from four mātrās (beats) to 16 mātrās.

following.text: It is hoped that learners will carry these alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) through, beginning from every note, will extend their ascending order into a full ascent and descent, and will practise them. Then, if possible, they will also try to make other similar alaṅkāras on the basis of the elements contained in them.
